subsection: 6. The State in France: monarchy, republic and Empire, 1815–1871

notes.h: The restored Bourbons and the Charter, 1814–1830
notes.b: After Napoleon's first abdication the Bourbon monarchy was restored, but it accepted a constitution. Its later refusal to respect that constitution brought the July Revolution of 1830.
points: Louis XVIII returned to the throne in 1814 and issued the Charter (Charte constitutionnelle), which kept many Napoleonic institutions and set up a two-chamber legislature.
The franchise under the Charter was very narrow: only men who paid high direct taxes could vote, so the electorate was a small minority of wealthy property owners.
Louis XVIII's government carried out a White Terror in 1815 against Bonapartists and Revolutionaries, with lists of suspects and summary punishments in the south.
Charles X succeeded in 1824 and tried to restore the authority of the Church and the nobility, passing a law on sacrilege and compensating the émigrés.
The elections of 1827 returned a liberal opposition majority against the government, and in August 1829 Charles X appointed Prince Polignac, whose ministry lacked support in the chamber.
On 25 July 1830 Charles X issued the July Ordinances, which dissolved the Chamber, restricted the press and changed the electoral rules.
Paris rose on 27–29 July 1830 (the Three Glorious Days), and Charles X abdicated and went into exile in Britain.
The liberal deputies chose Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, as King of the French, which made the monarchy a constitutional one with a middle-class character.
The franchise was extended a little, but only about 240,000 men could vote, so power stayed with wealthy property owners.
François Guizot, the leading minister from 1840 to 1848, opposed any further extension of the vote and said that the enrichment of the country should be the aim of its citizens.
The opposition used the banquet campaign of 1847–48, public dinners at which reform was demanded, to put pressure on the government.
Guizot banned a banquet planned for Paris in February 1848, and the ban led directly to the crowds that brought down the July Monarchy.

notes.h: The February Revolution and the Second Republic, 1848
points: Fighting in Paris on 22–24 February 1848 brought barricades and the defection of the National Guard, and Louis-Philippe abdicated on 24 February.
A provisional government was proclaimed the Second Republic on 24 February 1848, with the poet Alphonse de Lamartine as one of its leading members.
The provisional government granted universal male suffrage on 2 March 1848, which increased the electorate to about 9 million men.
National Workshops (Ateliers nationaux) were set up in late February 1848 to give work to the unemployed, which increased the cost to the government.
The National Workshops were closed in June 1848, and workers resisted the closure with the June Days (23–26 June 1848), an insurrection in Paris.
General Louis-Eugène Cavaignac crushed the June Days with troops, leading to many deaths and arrests, and he was given emergency powers for a time.
A constitution of November 1848 established a presidency with a four-year term and a single-chamber Legislative Assembly.
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, nephew of Napoleon I, was elected president on 10 December 1848 with a large majority of the vote, beating Cavaignac.
Louis-Napoléon had been imprisoned at Ham after an attempted rising at Boulogne in 1840, and he had lived in exile in Britain before 1848.
The Party of Order, made up of monarchists and conservatives, won a large majority in the Legislative Assembly elections of May 1849.
The Falloux Law (March 1850) gave the Catholic Church a major role in education, and in May 1850 the conservative majority restricted the franchise, removing about three million voters.
Louis-Napoléon's campaign to change the constitution to allow his re-election failed in the Assembly in July 1851.

notes.h: The coup and the Second Empire, 1851–1860
points: On 2 December 1851 Louis-Napoléon carried out a coup d'état, arresting deputies and dissolving the Assembly, and armed resistance in Paris and the provinces was suppressed.
A plebiscite in December 1851 approved the coup and gave the president extended powers, and the plebiscite of November 1852 approved the restoration of the empire.
Louis-Napoléon proclaimed the Second Empire on 2 December 1852 and took the name Napoleon III, with the title of Emperor of the French.
The Second Empire in its early years was authoritarian: the press was censored, political opponents were exiled, and elections were controlled by official candidates.
The Crédit Mobilier, founded in 1852, financed railways, industry and urban development, and rapid economic growth followed in the 1850s.
The Paris Exposition of 1855 and the rebuilding of Paris under Haussmann showed the regime's commitment to modern economy and prestige.

notes.h: The liberal Empire and foreign policy, 1860–1870
points: The Cobden–Chevalier Treaty of 1860 with Britain reduced French tariffs, opening French markets to British goods and encouraging French industry to modernise.
In 1860–63 the regime gave the legislature more freedom to debate, and in 1864 it legalised the right to strike, though collective action remained restricted.
France fought in the Crimean War (1853–56) as Britain's ally and it helped Piedmont in 1859, which led to the French gains of Nice and Savoy in 1860.
French forces in Mexico, under Napoleon III's plan to create a French-backed empire, were withdrawn in 1867, and the Habsburg Archduke Maximilian was executed by the Mexican republicans.
Napoleon III's government lost prestige after the Austrian war of 1866 and the Prussian victory, which had changed the balance of power in Europe.
Émile Ollivier formed a liberal ministry in 1870, and a plebiscite in May 1870 approved a more liberal constitution for the Empire.

notes.b: Napoleon III was a participant in the political events of 1848 to 1870 and a symbol of the French regime. Contemporaries and historians disagree about whether he was a modernising leader or an autocrat who led France into disaster.
points: Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte was born in Paris in 1808, the son of Louis Bonaparte, King of Holland, and the nephew of Napoleon I.
He attempted coups in Strasbourg (1836) and Boulogne (1840), both of which failed, and he spent six years in prison at Ham before escaping in 1846.
As president of the Second Republic he won the election of December 1848 by appealing to peasants and to the memory of his uncle, and he was supported by conservatives who expected to use him.
His coup of December 1851 and the Second Empire that followed made him the central political figure in France until 1870.
In foreign policy he backed Piedmont in 1859, joined the Crimean War, supported the Mexican adventure and then led France into war with Prussia in 1870.
He was captured at Sedan on 2 September 1870, and he was held in Germany before going into exile in Britain, where he died in 1873.
Contemporaries were divided: supporters praised economic growth and Paris, while republicans and liberals such as Victor Hugo denounced him as a usurper.
Historians now stress his interest in social reform, his economic programme and his attempts at liberal reform, though they also judge his foreign policy as a failure.

notes.h: Key personality: Victor Hugo, opponent and exile
notes.b: Hugo was a politician as well as a writer. His political role in this period was as a deputy and an opponent of the Empire; his literary work is covered in the notes on cultural nationalism.
points: Victor Hugo, born in 1802, was a leading Romantic writer and a monarchist in the 1820s, and he had become a republican by 1848.
He was elected to the Constituent Assembly of 1848 and the Legislative Assembly, where he defended freedom of the press and education and opposed the restriction of the franchise.
He opposed Louis-Napoléon's presidency and was one of the leaders of the democratic opposition in the Legislative Assembly after 1849.
After the coup of December 1851 he was forced to leave France, first to Brussels, then to the Channel Islands, where he lived in exile until 1870.
His pamphlet Napoléon le Petit (1852) and his satirical poems Les Châtiments (1853) attacked Napoleon III and made him a symbol of republican resistance.
He refused an amnesty offered in 1859 and stayed in exile on Guernsey as a protest against the regime.
Hugo returned to Paris in September 1870 after the proclamation of the Third Republic.
Contemporaries saw him as a republican hero, while critics saw his politics as inconsistent, and historians now recognise him as a principled defender of liberty and democracy.

notes.h: Sedan, the Third Republic and the Paris Commune
points: After Sedan the Empire collapsed, and a republic was proclaimed in Paris on 4 September 1870 by deputies from Paris, including Léon Gambetta.
A Government of National Defence continued the war against Prussia from Paris, and the city was besieged from September 1870 to January 1871.
The National Assembly elected in February 1871 was dominated by monarchists and was based in Versailles, not in Paris.
The Paris Commune of 18 March to 28 May 1871 was a revolutionary government of Parisian radicals and socialists, which was suppressed by government troops in the Bloody Week.
The Third Republic was confirmed in 1875 by constitutional laws, which established a parliamentary system with a president.

Five regime changes between 1814 and 1870 (the Bourbon Restoration, the July Monarchy, the Second Republic, the Second Empire and the Third Republic) reflected the lack of agreement about the basis of government.
The Bourbon and July regimes were limited by narrow franchises, and the exclusion of most men from political life made opposition likely.
The Second Republic showed that universal male suffrage could bring a president who would destroy the republic, and it deepened the divide between the urban poor and the conservative countryside.
The Second Empire gave France economic growth and prestige but depended on the personal authority of Napoleon III, and its foreign policy failures weakened it.

Assessment: France's regimes were unstable because each one lacked a broad consensus, and the authority of the state rested on the personal position of its rulers rather than on a settled constitutional system.

keyTerms.definition: The constitution granted by Louis XVIII in 1814, which kept many Napoleonic institutions and set up a two-chamber legislature with a narrow franchise.
The decrees of 25 July 1830 by Charles X that dissolved the Chamber and restricted the press, which triggered the July Revolution.
The constitutional monarchy of Louis-Philippe from 1830 to 1848, with a narrow franchise and power concentrated among wealthy property owners.
The state schemes set up in February 1848 to give work to the unemployed, which were closed in June 1848 and provoked the June Days.
The insurrection of 23–26 June 1848 in Paris, provoked by the closure of the National Workshops and crushed by General Cavaignac.
Louis-Napoléon's seizure of power, which dissolved the Assembly and led to a plebiscite approving the extended powers of the president.
The regime of Napoleon III from 1852 to 1870, first authoritarian and later more liberal, which ended with defeat at Sedan.
The doctrine favouring constitutional government, civil liberties and limits on the power of rulers, which the July Monarchy and the Charter claimed to uphold.
Government by the people through elected representatives, which in France meant universal male suffrage from 1848.
A system in which a single ruler holds unlimited power, which Napoleon III's authoritarian Empire represented in its early years.
The revolutionary government of Paris from 18 March to 28 May 1871, suppressed by government troops in the Bloody Week.

factCards.definition: Louis XVIII issued the Charter in 1814, setting up a two-chamber legislature with a narrow franchise of wealthy men.

factCards.definition: On 25 July 1830 Charles X issued decrees that dissolved the Chamber and restricted the press, which led to the revolution of 27–29 July.
The liberal deputies chose Louis-Philippe, Duke of Orléans, as King of the French after Charles X abdicated.

factCards.term: Guizot's ban on the banquet, February 1848
factCards.definition: Guizot's ban on a Paris banquet in February 1848 led to the street protests that toppled the July Monarchy.
The Provisional Government introduced universal male suffrage on 2 March 1848, enlarging the electorate to about nine million men.
The closure of the National Workshops in June 1848 provoked the June Days, a workers' insurrection in Paris.
Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte was elected president on 10 December 1848 with a large majority of the vote.
The 1850 law on Catholic education, passed by the conservative majority of the Assembly, which also restricted the franchise.

factCards.term: Proclamation of the Second Empire, 2 December 1852
factCards.definition: Louis-Napoléon took the name Napoleon III and the title of Emperor of the French on 2 December 1852.
The 1860 trade agreement with Britain that reduced French tariffs and opened French markets to British goods.
The 1864 law that legalised the right to strike in France, though collective action remained restricted.
Victor Hugo went into exile after the coup of December 1851, living in Brussels and then on Jersey and Guernsey until 1870.
Victor Hugo's pamphlet attacking Napoleon III, written from exile and published in 1852.
A republic was proclaimed in Paris on 4 September 1870, after the defeat at Sedan and the collapse of the Second Empire.
The revolutionary government of Paris, which was suppressed by government troops in the Bloody Week at the end of May 1871.
